센서가 기록하는 값은 반사율이 아니라\n\n$$DN(\\lambda) =:
The value recorded by the sensor is not reflectance.

$$DN(\lambda) = R(\lambda)\,E(\lambda)\,S(\lambda) + d(\lambda)$$

It is. $E$ is the lighting, $S$ is the sensor sensitivity, and $d$ is the **added offset** such as dark and path radiation.

**Sensor Dark** — Block the lens and first subtract the measured value from all images and panels with the same integration time·gain. Even if there is only one panel, the absolute reflectance can be calculated as $R = R_{panel}(DN-D)/(DN_{panel}-D)$.

**When there is no Dark file** — If you have prior confirmation that the sensor dark is approximately flat across wavelengths, you can temporarily use a manual constant value (default DN 100). In this case, a history of synthetic Dark usage will remain in the results.

**Two or more panels** — For each band, $R=a(\lambda)(DN-D)$ is adjusted to all valid panels simultaneously. As bright panels approach saturation, their weights are gently lowered, and normal, low-reflectance panels take over the same regression equation. By not cutting and pasting panel spectra, discontinuities at transition boundaries can be reduced.

**Common Interval Verification** — Check with CV how well each correction coefficient matches at a wavelength where multiple panels are all normal. If the difference is large, you should check panel height, angle, contamination, or lighting changes.

**Panel Selection Tips** — Pick ones that cover the reflectance range of the object of interest. Vegetation NIR goes up to 40-60%, so a bright panel is needed, and shadows and soil are 5-10%, so a dark panel is needed for that section to be interpolated, not extrapolated.
